title: In his documentary, Brian DePalma says that he uses a lot of Hitchockian visuals because Hitchcock invented a visual language and nobody took advantage of it. What other directors do you think have a specific visual language that could be reused?

commenti.body: [removed]

Eisenstein, Pudovkin, Dovzhenko, Jean Epstein, Germaine Dulac, Dmitri Kirsanoff, Mario Peixoto, Carl Dreyer

Don’t see too much of their techniques used these days. Maybe in moments but certainly not in in any prolonged way. At least not that I’m aware of. Having said that, I don’t watch many modern films…

Among modern directors I guess Sion Sono has his own style. Tsukamoto too. And Tetsuya Nakashima.

She borrows from the silent Soviet directors heavily, but Lynne Ramsay has an incredible cinematic vocabulary that I have never seen a single other person use except for Jean Marc Valle, and that was only with the Sharp Objects miniseries.

The entire story of her films are almost entirely delivered through the visuals, and dialogue has barely any emphasis placed on it, and at points completely fades into background noise or goes totally silent. 

She makes heavy use of a technique which she calls “quick pops” in her scripts, which are when a single image pops on screen for just a moment that doesn’t appear to have context until much later, and she drip feeds them slowly throughout the story to inform who the characters are, where they’ve been and what they’re going to do all at once. Almost like time is cyclical. 

She uses image juxtaposition and image in a wholly unique way, imo. While some directors spend entire scenes of expository dialogue to explain something, Ramsay often just used a single shot that lasts 2 seconds. 

You could literally watch her films without sound and still understand everything even though in some cases (like We Need to Talk About Kevin) the story is anything but straightforward. There’s not a single living filmmaker who I can recall who does this on the scale the Ramsay does. 

I think the reason that many could learn from her/ utilise those tools is because she is so economic with her filmmaking. Stop wasting time telling me that something happens when you can just show me. 

I think in general, many films are far too long and something like this could absolutely help with that. It also has the benefit of being a uniquely cinematic approach, where as other means often evoke the tools of other mediums like theatre and literature.

Bob Fosse’s staging, composition, and often quick-cut editing style is exhilarating and kinetic in ways that I’ve rarely experienced from other major directors.  Cabaret, Lenny, All That Jazz, and to a lesser degree, Star 80, to me feel as fresh and innovative today as they did when I first saw them years ago.

Nic Roeg’s 70s films are masterpieces of elliptical disjointed, nonlinear editing, deconstructed narratives, and a visual style that often made use of snap zooms in or out to heighten drama and draw attention to important story points.  The wiki entry on Nic Roeg does a very good and insightful summation of his innovative style.  As with Fosse, I’m still blown away by Roeg’s mastery of the craft.

Robert Altman’s signature technique of an almost always slowly zooming in and out camera, usually combined with a lateral tracking dolly shot has, to my knowledge, almost never been duplicated, except by his protégé, director Alan Rudolph, who worked as an AD on a number of occasions of Altman’s signature films.

I love Fosse so much, and what strikes me about his films is that it's not one thing that he does, it's everything. The editing, the blocking, the movement, the camera, everything is this perfect quilt, nothing stands out because everything stands out, if that makes sense. A lot of directors really put stock in just one thing and that becomes their trademark, but Fosse uses the full cinematic package.

Also, I don't think there's another director who can film the human body that well. I have this aesthetic fascination with the body and all the weird poses and movements that we do that often aren't in film, and Fosse just gets that. A big part of that is obviously his coreography, but even just how he shoots people moving is great.

BTW You didn't mention *Sweet Charity*, don't know if you've seen it, but the dance scenes in that movie are unquestionably [the best he ever did](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DSSlWfOCgLw). Pure self-indulgence, I don't care, give it all to me.

Kurosawa made use of advanced blocking that combined many takes into one, a style that is sometimes also called editing in camera. The only contemporary director who took full advantage of this technique that I can think of is actually Spielberg. There is a modern trend to show off impossible long takes, sometimes stretching to feature length (thanks to digital filming). But I don't count those, since I find the artistic purpose behind them mostly questionable.

>Kurosawa made use of advanced blocking that combined many takes into one, a style that is sometimes also called editing in camera.

Can you explain this bit? I haven't watched much Kurosawa yet (just *Rashomon* and *Yojimbo*, cause I'm a basic ass bitch), so I'm curious to hear more about this.

>There is a modern trend to show off impossible long takes, sometimes stretching to feature length (thanks to digital filming).

I agree, they were cool when the trend started, but now they are just getting a little too "Look at me! I know how to make the movies!"

Ironically though, I'm Portuguese and Portuguese films are infamous for never moving the camera, which I also don't like that approach. I feel as though there should be a measured approach in between.

It could be said for a lot of experimental directors, but Stan Brakhage, as far as I'm concerned, is the quintessential reference for "creating a new visual language". It's not really reproducible in mainstream movies, but watching his work has totally changed the way I see and consider any piece of cinema.
So glad someone else is stanning Ramsay.

I'm not the OP, but there's one camera move in particular that Kurosawa used over and over which is where it goes from a dolly crash close up, to a close up, to an over the shoulder, without cutting. 

There are many examples but one that comes to the top of my head is this one in [Hidden Fortress](https://dp0rksi384o97.cloudfront.net/exports/378a6b8e-c7ce-40b8-840a-a378b777efd0.gif?Policy=eyJTdGF0ZW1lbnQiOlt7IlJlc291cmNlIjoiaHR0cHM6XC9cL2RwMHJrc2kzODRvOTcuY2xvdWRmcm9udC5uZXRcL2V4cG9ydHNcLzM3OGE2YjhlLWM3Y2UtNDBiOC04NDBhLWEzNzhiNzc3ZWZkMC5naWYiLCJDb25kaXRpb24iOnsiRGF0ZUxlc3NUaGFuIjp7IkFXUzpFcG9jaFRpbWUiOjE3MTczMjY3MzJ9fX1dfQ__&Signature=d4LI2GHxTSZIi2xDGbC15-zPeDg2dNuncBCrrAo8cDTHko0CfJenoAn20bG6gdq3PzmBJhy6w39l4rQC9vw-M2KQjRS3Mzp9XU3Y880~w6YXTac2nvQ9UeEcJkHi0qNdtJc6JhCPtZfCIF982tCL~SnBDgITv9~jFT94a~1XMGRticVCOcwNliFkqx1CGWIu~vDdWupBTi9r3lWiskv45e4vOdpghHLWrt5Anvb2O5Cxx~4KbqiOvh2-kXbCIPSCHbMQm7v25l95ex38N-sme25h~T~oPudvsLXh5c4jok149s-gaQukF9L-oWC94umJ69m5Y1cYgBaGw2d1uaL3lw__&Key-Pair-Id=APKAIWQDLHITBKTFWBJA)

Yeah, maybe I'm not good at explaining things. Imagine a conventional director who uses cuts to draw your eyes. First, he establishes a group of people in a wide shot, then he shows the close-up of a face, then cuts to a reaction shot. Kurosawa would do all this in one single take with a combination of moving the actors as well as the camera, making the scene more emotionally compelling.

I'm not big on the avant-garde, but there are two avant-garde works that use techniques I wish I saw more often. Jonas Mekas's "As I was Moving Ahead etc" uses on-the-cutting-room-floor type footage for pretty much all the transitions, and it works beautifully. Secondly, in David Lynch's "Twin Peaks: The Return", he sometimes juxtaposes a very-low-framerate POV with a very-high-framerate POV. I have no idea what he was getting at here (definitely need to rewatch it some day) but it's one of the most memorable parts of the show, for me

Sam Esmail definitely has his own visual language: characters that are located on the sides of wide shots, dialogue shots that emphasize distance and disconnection through placement of the actors, lots of high-angle or low-angle visual shots that make the world seem off-kilter. It’s a very distinctive style, but influenced by film noir, so it’s a language that could be adapted by others.

100% agree on Fosse.  Brilliant director on every level.  

I like Sweet Charity, but to me, his three subsequent films are his masterpieces where he really came into his own and fully developed his style.  

I long ago lost track of how many times
I’ve seen Cabaret, Lenny, and All That Jazz, but every time I revisit them, I can feel my pulse quicken from the sheer kineticism — the camera movement and/or movement of bodies in static and      moving shots, the frequent rapid-fire editing that propels a scene, sequence, or the narrative forward — and I marvel at how quickly he seemed to master the medium.  It didn’t hurt that he had amazing DPs and editors working with him. 

Lenny is my personal favorite and my contender for best biopic ever (only Raging Bull comes close); the semi-nonlinear but never confusing editing enhances the drama, the gritty b&w cinematography, Dustin Hoffman’s best performance, the subject matter, the tragic ending (Fosse really loved a bleak conclusion, as do I)… just wow.

But I could also go on and on about Cabaret — every Cabaret number is perfection, the intercutting of the Emcee doing the slap dance on stage and the Nazis beating the club owner in the alley stuns me every time (starting with the abrupt and exciting cut away from the previous scene just as Liza yells “Now!” to cue Michael York to scream as the train rumbles by), the brief cutaway to the Emcee nodding and smiling sinisterly at the camera, as Michael York and Helmut Griem drive away from the Nazis singing in the Biergarten… just wow again!

Can’t fail to mention Fosse’s unparalleled audience cutaways in Cabaret and Lenny.  

Where to even begin with All That Jazz?  Ah, you’ve seen it, you know it’s great;)

I like Star 80 a lot, but to me it feels… cheaper? than his 70s films.  Sven Nykvist is a great cinematographer but here the lighting feels very tv movie-ish to me.  And the brutal, tragic, relentlessly unpleasant true story narrative is hard for me to watch, even as I acknowledge that Fosse was correct to depict it this way.

If you haven’t read Sam Wasson’s Fosse biography, it’s packed with insight into Fosse’s process.

Anyway, TL;DR: Fosse rules! His movies rule!  And he’s one of my top five all-time favorite directors.

I love Fosse's style also. I do think, however, that he took it too far in All That Jazz. It's a brilliant film, but the editing, while often dazzling, is too much - too frenetic - too busy. Love it or hate it, Altman often used a "fly on the wall" style and did the same with the mic by just burying it somewhere so he could get an atmosphere of pure spontaniety and realism. I think it worked a lot of the time and sometimes felt awkward.

Nobody understood movement like Fosse. When you're watching his films you get the feeling he's obsessed with bodies moving through space - like he feels it on some abstract level beyond intellect. And he's so good at communicating this passion, we get to feel it too, we get to feel movement in the way he did. What a gift - thank you Fosse!

(BTW - I think you get a similar depiction of movement in the dance scenes in West Side Story which were directed by Fosse's mentor Jerome Robbins. The number 'Cool' especially gives me a similar vibe.)

We might differ on this topic, but what is the artistic purpose of a 10 to 20-minute long shot, other than showing off that you are capable of impressing an audience? And yeah, I like magic tricks like everybody, but if you know how it's done, even those lose their magic. I think Hitchcock said it best when he described his endeavor with Rope: “I undertook Rope as a stunt; that's the only way I can describe it.”

The idea that all extended takes fall in to the category of "showing off" is incredibly silly. Just because you can't comprehend why a shot would be that long does not mean the filmmakers intention is necessarily to show off.

I consider this a failure of imagination on your part. Something can be showy, while also having substance.

Of course there are instances of directors using it merely to show off, and that may be it's most common use. But it's certainly not inherent.
please, I didn't say "all extended takes".

I think the technique of something like *Mothlight* is a new cinematic language: eschewing the use of the camera entirely to create images by pressing objects like moth wings between strips of film. To literally turn filmmaking into a physical collage involving the celluloid itself is, I think, a radically new cinematic language.
Re: Portuguese films, I think *Francisca* (1981) made incredibly effective use of the still camera, turning scenes into *tableaux vivants* that visually reflect the characters' ennui.

One filmmaker not mentioned in this thread who clearly created his own (minimalistic) visual language: Yasujiro Ozu. 

In the words of the late, great David Bordwell:

>Every viewer would agree that Ozu succeeded in creating a distinctive approach to visual design: upright shapes and parallel lines arranged for balance across the frame; a tendency toward bilateral symmetry on the vertical axis; static elements near the edges of the frame which introduce graphic equivalences or tensions. But the distinctiveness of the Ozu shot owes most to a single, highly controversial framing choice. The urge to make every image sharp, stable, and striking is the 'dominant' of each shot, and as always in art the dominant deforms all the techniques under its sway. The most remarkable and puzzling deformation takes place in the choice of camera position. Recall some critical commonplaces. Ozu is said to employ a low camera angle, setting the camera two to three feet off the ground. This is said to be a constant, unvarying position. Most critics assert that this represents the eye-level view of a person seated on the floor, the 'traditional' vantage point of the Japanese kneeling on a tatami mat. Some writers identify it as the viewpoint of a child, or a god, or a dog, or even the seated movie audience.21 It is also sometimes said that Ozu's camera position is a convention of the home-drama genre, or part of a wider stylistic trend to which several directors belonged. In all respects these claims are questionable. Most often, it is true, the shot is in some sense 'low', though Ozu will occasionally employ high angles of landscapes. But he does not shoot from a low camera angle. Almost always the camera is level, or tipped only a few degrees up from a horizontal axis. (Compare fig. 1, a genuine low angle from Walk Cheerfully, with virtually any other frame in this book.) What makes Ozu's camera seem 'low' is not its angle but its height. And that height is not fixed at two feet, three feet, or any particular distance. Ozu's rule is to set the lens axis between halfway and two-thirds of the way down the object to be filmed.
That's a pretty crude way to evaluate form or judge cinema, imo. It's a story about a guy and I don't have deeper thematic insight than that.

I think there’s something to be said for how filmmakers around the transition from black and white to full color *used* color. Now it’s just natural that everything is in color and no one gives it a second thought. But if you look at a lot of directors that made black and white movies and you’ll see them using color as a tool for story telling.

A favorite example of mine is Amira Kurosawa’s Ran. The battle scenes in particular have this dark background to them which contrasts starkly with the soldiers in bright colors in the foreground which makes the entire scene pop out at you. It’s rather striking and I’d love to see more thought put into the use of color in modern movies. Especially in movies focusing on warfare in older periods of history……. Generally speaking older military forces were quite colorful.

Raimi is one of my favourite directors of all time so I am biased, but honestly I think the reason you don't see a lot of people aping his style is because, well, all those quintessential Raimi-isms are incredibly inventive and creative and I honestly don't think many directors actually have the ability or the idiosycratic vision of Raimi. That may sound like I am overstating it, but if you ever listen to Raimi talk about all the out of the box, crazy inventive things he did with cameras and camer techniques to achieve very particular shots, you really are just left with a sense of 'how the fuck did he even think of that? How did he envision a shot like that and then actually figure out how to achieve it like that?' (Especially when we are talking about his earlier films where he had next to no budget and no resources!)
